messages.subject: More questions on two-bel methods
parts:
Dear Dr. Buckland,
Thank you very much for your answer. I woukd like to ask you some
additional questions about our work.
First, I have followed your suggestions and I have observed that the
upper limit for the outer band has a very weak influenfe on the density
estimate (I have tried with 75, 100 and 150 m) and that estimates
obtained with DISTANCE were very similar to the estimates obtained by
the direct formulas for 2 belts.
The data set I'm analyzing includes the repeated counting (of
Moustached Warblers, Acrocephalus melanopogon) on the same transects (in
reedbeds) once per week. We want to obtain a single estimate of density
for the breeding season combining the transects of april and may. I
remember to have read in the 1993 book that this could be done by
pooling the data of all transects and estimating density as if they had
been obtained from one single transect with length multiplied by the
number of repetitions. My question is if this procedure would be correct
to estimate density and its SE, or if there is a better way to obtain
these estimates.
Thank you very much for your help
Best wishes
Germ=E1n L=F3pez

> > I'm analyzing some transect data obtained with the two belt
method.
> > Birds deteected were classified just as within 25 m of distance or out

> > of this band.
For point transects, this is given on p204-5 of the 2001 distance
sampling book. (It's also in the 1993 book.) The maths doesn't work
out
so nicely for line transects - see the reference to Jarvinen and
Vaisanen
on p206. For the half-normal model, you have to use numerical methods,
so
the easy solution is to use Distance with 2 distance bands, giving some
upper limit for the outer band. 100m might work OK for smaller species
-
try different choices, based on estimates of the maximum distance a
species is potentially detectable, and see if estimation is sensitive to

this choice.

Steve Buckland
